newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN refugee chief fears wider crisis in east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UN refugee chief fears wider crisis in east Zaire.

text.p: U.N. refugee agency chief Sadako Ogata, back from a whirlwind tour of central Africa's troubled Great Lakes region, said on Tuesday she feared eastern Zaire's humanitarian crisis would widen and called for an end to government air raids on rebel-held towns.

Ogata said thousands of refugees including Zaireans were fleeing to Uganda, Tanzania and Zambia, uprooted by a war intertwined with the ethnic Hutu-Tutsi conflict in Rwanda, where the Hutu army and militia killed up to 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994 before fleeing en masse into Zaire.
"Is this region settled? No. There's a new outflow of refugees. We'll have to expect diverse developments," Ogata told a news conference. "The security situation is very worrying."
The war escalated on Monday with Zairean air raids on the rebel-held towns of Shabunda, Walikale and Bukavu, where aid workers reported at least 21 people killed.
Ogata called for an end to the air raids, saying they threatened Western relief operations for the refugees.
"I hope this kind of attacks does not take place," she said. "All our operations suffer when there is any intensification of military operations."
Ogata said east Zaire's biggest refugee settlement sheltering 200,000 Rwandan Hutus in Tingi-Tingi risked becoming a battleground with the arming of Hutu militiamen.
She urged the West to help remove the Hutu militiamen.

"With the transport of ammunition and pace of militarisation of the (Tingi-Tingi) camp...armed elements must be separated. If the camp becomes militarised, it'll become a base for offensives and a target for counter-offensives," she said.

"All those bringing in things to the camp and those involved in military activity must stop this and I hope the international community will support this," said Ogata. "There are a lot of civilians in that camp, women and children."

Ogata has long been lobbying the West to help rescue the refugees and has accused the international community of opting for a quick-fix and losing interest in their plight. There have been few signs so far that anyone is prepared to help.
She said the refugees, who are surviving on supplies flown into the remote area by aid agencies, were in a very bad state.
"Left to themselves without major assistance coming in, there will be more than usual deaths," she said.
The UNHCR chief conceded that security assurances would be hard to obtain to repatriate the refugees amidst the war.
"This is a war zone. It is very difficult to assure the movement of aid workers, or food and transport, " she said.
"Assuring security through a very complicated frontline area requires everybody's support."
